title: Kioxia Stock Plunge Makes It Japan's Cheapest Blue Chip
summary: Kioxia's 40% November crash drove its valuation to 1.7x forward earnings, making it Japan's cheapest Nikkei 225 stock amid AI chip market uncertainty.
body_markdown:
**Officially launched on November 26, 2026.**


#### 💡 TL;DR


- Kioxia stock crashed 40% in November 2026, trading at 1.7x forward earnings, the lowest valuation in Japan's Nikkei 225 index.
- Analysts maintain 18 buy ratings despite AI market uncertainty, citing sold-out 2027 production and long-term chip supply agreements.
- Bulls see rebound potential from extreme undervaluation while bears cite AI spending doubts and high price-to-book ratio at 4.2x.


Kioxia Holdings has become Japan's cheapest blue-chip stock after a brutal 40% selloff in November 2026, with shares now trading at just 1.7 times forward earnings estimates. The Japanese memory chipmaker's valuation collapse, driven by investor concerns over AI infrastructure spending sustainability, has pushed it below Tokyo Electric Power to the bottom of the Nikkei 225 index.


## Availability and Market Impact


Officially trading at these historic lows as of November 26, 2026, Kioxia's stock has become cheaper than[SK Hynix](https://emergent.sh/news/sk-hynix-becomes-kioxia-s-top-shareholder-ai) and all major memory chip peers on a forward earnings basis. The company's market capitalization has cratered despite management disclosure that 2027 production is completely sold out and over half of projected 2028 shipments are already under contract.


Analysts highlight the disconnect between fundamentals and market price. "I have never seen, historically, a company generating this level of profit trade at such a low valuation," said Kazuyoshi Saito, senior analyst at Iwai Cosmo Securities. The sell-side maintains overwhelming support with 18 buy ratings versus one hold and one sell.


## What Drove the Collapse


The November selloff accelerated after Kioxia issued unexpectedly conservative guidance on chip prices and profitability earlier this month. Near-term headwinds include uncertainty over Big Tech's ability to fund massive AI infrastructure buildouts and potential political resistance to data center expansion.


Double-digit daily price swings have become routine as retail investors unwind leveraged positions. "Unless there are clear signs that cloud providers will continue to invest aggressively, it will be difficult for the stock to rebound," warned Takumi Nishida, fund manager at Asset Management One.


SMBC Nikko Securities analyst Takeru Hanaya notes that Kioxia's conservative pricing assumptions may reflect near-term shifts toward lower-margin smartphone chips while premium data-center shipments face delays.


## Bull Case for Recovery


Despite market pessimism, structural factors support a rebound thesis. Kioxia announced in October 2026 that it will return 100% of excess cash to shareholders over the medium to long term, with an interim dividend already declared. Speculation about subsidiary dividends funding a major share buyback drove the stock up by its daily limit on Thursday.


SK Kim of Daiwa Securities argues the valuation floor has been reached: "It's fair to say the stock is already at or near a bottom at current levels. It's unlikely for the valuation to fall much further from here."


Bulls point to long-term supply agreements locking in elevated chip prices and management's track record of conservative guidance. The company's production capacity is essentially pre-sold through 2027, providing revenue visibility that the current 1.7x earnings multiple fails to reflect.


## Valuation Complexity


Not all metrics paint Kioxia as deeply undervalued. The stock trades at 4.2 times book value, more than double Samsung's valuation and higher than most Nikkei 225 constituents. Some investors view price-to-book as a more reliable metric for cyclical memory chipmakers than forward earnings multiples.


This valuation gap explains why sophisticated institutional buyers remain cautious despite analyst enthusiasm. The memory chip sector's notorious cyclicality and current AI market volatility create legitimate uncertainty about whether today's earnings power will persist.


## What This Means


Kioxia's transformation into Japan's cheapest major stock represents a dramatic shift in market sentiment around AI infrastructure investments. The 40% November decline reflects broader doubts about whether cloud hyperscalers can sustain the capital spending required for ambitious AI projects. For value investors willing to bet on a multi-year AI buildout and improved shareholder returns, the current 1.7x forward earnings multiple presents a potential entry point. However, persistent volatility and uncertainty around Big Tech AI spending commitments suggest the near-term path remains treacherous. The stock's fate hinges on whether 2027 earnings materialize as management projects and whether investors regain confidence in the sustainability of AI infrastructure demand.
